name: Samaritanism
info: Samaritanism is the Abrahamic monotheistic ethnic religion of the Samaritan people, who hold Mount Gerizim to be God's holy place and the Torah their only scripture; it took shape as a distinct tradition in the Hasmonean and Roman era.

facts.origin: Samaria, around Mount Gerizim. Samaritans trace their separate history to a schism in the time of the High Priest Eli; scholars see a distinct tradition emerging in the Hasmonean and Roman era, with the temple on Gerizim built in the 5th century BCE.
facts.founder: none: Samaritanism holds itself to be the faith the Israelites kept under Moses, whom it regards as the final prophet; after him the only authority is the successive Samaritan priesthood, from the line of Aaron.
facts.scriptures: The Samaritan Pentateuch (the Torah), the only scripture; Samaritans also keep a variation of the Book of Joshua, which they do not regard as scripture, and chronicles, halakhic texts, midrash and liturgy.

t: Samaritans hold that there is one God, YHWH, that the Torah given to Moses is the only true holy book, and that Mount Gerizim, not Jerusalem, is the place God chose.

Scholars see Samaritanism as taking shape as a distinct tradition in the Hasmonean and Roman era, after John Hyrcanus destroyed the Gerizim temple around 120 BCE; Samaritan tradition traces the separation to a schism in the time of the High Priest Eli.
About 900 registered communal Samaritans remain in 2025; they take this small number to be the fulfilment of a scriptural prophecy and hope for the Taheb, the Restorer.
dyk: Samaritans hold that the Binding of Isaac took place on Mount Gerizim, not at Jerusalem's Temple Mount, and in their version of the Ten Commandments the tenth commands an altar to be built on Gerizim.
ev: The Hasmonean ruler and high priest John Hyrcanus destroys the temple on Mount Gerizim and brings Samaria under his control

sections.origins:
Samaritanism holds itself to be the truly preserved form of the monotheistic faith that the Israelites kept under Moses. Samaritan historiography traces the separation of Samaritans and Jews to a period soon after the Israelites entered the Promised Land. In this account the High Priest Eli left Mount Gerizim, where stood the first Israelite altar in Canaan, and built a competing altar at Shiloh. Those who followed him later settled Jerusalem and became the Jews, while those who stayed on Gerizim, in Samaria, became the Samaritans. The 14th-century historian Abu'l-Fath tells of a civil war between Eli and the sons of Phinehas, and the Samaritan New Chronicle, believed to have been composed in the 18th century, says the Israelites divided into three groups in Eli's time.

Scholars give a different account. A genetic study of 2004 suggests that Samaritan lineages trace back to a common ancestor with Jews in the paternally inherited priesthood, close in time to the Assyrian conquest of the kingdom of Israel, and that the Samaritans are probably descendants of the historical Israelite population. The proto-Samaritans' religion was probably no different from that of Judea, and Samaritanism likely did not emerge as a distinct tradition until the Hasmonean and Roman era. The temple on Mount Gerizim was built in the 5th century BCE as one of many Yahwistic temples in Samaria, and a large building programme began around the 4th century BCE. Debates between Jews and Samaritans are attested from the 2nd century BCE.
sections.beliefs:
Samaritans believe in one God, called YHWH, the same God recognised by the Jewish prophets. They hold the Torah to be the only true holy book, given by God to Moses, whom they consider the final prophet; after him the only authority is the successive Samaritan priesthood, from the line of Aaron. For Samaritans Shechem, not Jerusalem, is the one sanctuary chosen by God, and they do not recognise the sanctity of Jerusalem or the Temple Mount. They believe that Mount Gerizim was where the Binding of Isaac took place. They also expect an apocalypse, the day of vengeance, at the end of days.

Samaritans hope for the Taheb, the Restorer, a figure from the tribe of Joseph. In their belief he will be a prophet like Moses for 40 years and bring back the Kingdom of Israel; the dead will be resurrected, and he will discover the Tabernacle, bring it to Mount Gerizim and be buried next to Joseph. They hold that he will perform three signs and that Gerizim will be restored to its former glory.

The Samaritans keep the sabbath from Friday to Saturday sundown with seven prayer services, and they celebrate Pesach, Shavuot and Sukkot by their own method of fixing the dates. Passover is particularly important and climaxes with the sacrifice of up to 40 sheep. During festivals the liturgy is recited with a preserved Samaritan Hebrew pronunciation of the Tetragrammaton.
sections.texts:
The Torah, in its Samaritan version, is the only scripture Samaritans accept; they reject the other books of the Tanakh and all later Jewish literature, such as the Talmud, the Midrash and the Tosefta. They have a variation of the Book of Joshua, but do not regard it as scripture. There are some 6,000 differences between the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Masoretic Jewish text, and by one estimate 1,900 points of agreement with the Greek LXX version. The variations, some corroborated by readings in the Old Latin, Syriac and Ethiopian translations, attest to the antiquity of the Samaritan text, although the exact date of its composition is still largely unclear. The Abisha Scroll is attributed to Abishua, grandson of Aaron, and traditionally compiled during the Bronze Age.

The most important differences concern the status of Mount Gerizim. In the Samaritan version of the Ten Commandments the tenth commands an altar to be built for God on Gerizim, and the Samaritan Pentateuch speaks of the place God has chosen, where the Jewish Torah has the place God will choose.

Samaritan law differs from rabbinic halakha. Historical writings include the Tolidah, the Chronicle of Joshua, the Adler chronicle and the Kitab al-Tarikh of Abu'l-Fath. Halakhic texts include the Hillukh and the 12th-century Kitab at-Tabbah. The Memar Markah, theological treatises attributed to Hakkam Markha, is dated to the 3rd or 4th century, and the legendary Aramaic Al-Asatir to the 11th and 12th.
sections.spread:
Samaritanism is an ethnic religion, the collective spiritual, cultural and legal tradition of the Samaritan people, who often prefer to be called Israelite Samaritans. Its centre is Mount Gerizim in Samaria, which Samaritans revere as the Israelites' original holy site. The temple there stood until the Hasmonean ruler and high priest John Hyrcanus destroyed it and brought Samaria under his control around 120 BCE.

That destruction led to a lasting sense of mutual hostility between Jews and Samaritans. From this point the Samaritans likely sought to distance themselves consciously from their Judean kin, and both peoples came to see the Samaritan faith as a religion distinct from Judaism. The relationship deteriorated with time, and by the time of Jesus Samaritans and Jews deeply disparaged one another, as the Parable of the Good Samaritan shows.

The Byzantine Empire persecuted the Samaritans, practically annihilating them after the Samaritan revolts of the 5th and 6th centuries. The Samaritan historian Benyamim Tsedaka traces the Samaritan custom of building the sukkah inside houses to persecution under the Byzantine Empire. In the present day the community has its own local priest at Holon in Israel, and in 2025 there are approximately 900 registered communal Samaritans.
sections.community:
The highest position in Samaritanism is the High Priest, chosen from the priestly caste, which is held to descend from the house of Aaron, brother of Moses. His residence is on Mount Gerizim, and since 1624 the oldest member of the priestly family has been chosen for the position. After him come the other priests, who usually wear a red turban and cassock, changing to more striking clothing on Saturdays and other sacred days. The community of Holon has its own local priest.

Samaritan custom prescribes that members of the priestly family do not work but deal only with religious matters, and that the rest of the community supports them through tithes and offerings. In 2003 the priestly family made up 28 percent of the community, so this arrangement has become impractical and its members now seek work like other Samaritans. From the priestly family come not only the priests but also the leaders of prayers (imams) and the rabbis, who teach the ancient Samaritan language. Samaritan synagogues are oriented toward Gerizim and usually stand on the outskirts of settlements.

Samaritans are not usually recognised as Jews by Orthodox Jews, especially rabbis, a rejection based on the accounts in the Books of Kings of the deportation of Israelites by Assyria around 720 BCE. The Babylonian Talmud says a Samaritan converting to Judaism must first renounce any belief in the sanctity of Gerizim, and that Samaritans should be treated as Jews where their practices are the same and as gentiles where they differ. Since the 19th century many Jews have considered Samaritans a Jewish sect.
sections.legacy:
The Gospels preserve the Parable of the Good Samaritan and other allusions showing that Jews and Samaritans did not associate with one another. Such stories refer to the relationship between Samaritanism and Judaism in the time of Jesus, not to the relationship between Samaritanism and Christianity. Relations with Christianity do not appear to have been entirely tolerant in the first Christian centuries, and the Byzantine Empire persecuted the Samaritans, practically annihilating them after the revolts of the 5th and 6th centuries.

Samaritanism remains a living tradition of about 900 registered communal Samaritans in 2025. Samaritans believe that this small population is a prophecy fulfilled, from a scriptural passage that says, “You will be left few in number.” Their faith keeps its own priesthood, its own sabbath and festival practice, and its own version of the Torah, which they regard as the true preserved form of the Israelites' faith.

Samaritans hope for a future time when the Taheb will perform three signs, an era of divine favour will return, the hidden tabernacle of Moses will be miraculously revealed, and Mount Gerizim will be restored to its former glory. Jews and Samaritans each hold that their own people kept the original faith of the Israelites, and each holds a different place to be the site of the Binding of Isaac.

summary: Samaritanism is the ethnic religion of the Samaritan people, centred on Mount Gerizim and the Samaritan Pentateuch. Samaritans hold it to be the faith the Israelites kept under Moses; scholars see a distinct tradition emerging in the Hasmonean and Roman era. About 900 registered communal Samaritans remain in 2025.
references: Robert T. Anderson, The Keepers: An Introduction to the History and Culture of the Samaritans (Hendrickson Publishing, 2002)
Gary N. Knoppers, Jews and Samaritans: The Origins and History of Their Early Relations (OUP USA, 2013)
R. J. Coggins, Samaritans and Jews: The Origins of Samaritanism Reconsidered (Basil Blackwell, 1975)
John Macdonald, The Theology of the Samaritans (SCM Press, 1964)
notes: Source: only the Samaritanism article, which is short; its Notes, Sources and Further reading lists are empty, so references are left empty.

Start -120 (circa): the article says Samaritanism likely did not emerge as a distinct tradition until the Hasmonean and Roman era and dates John Hyrcanus's destruction of the temple to around 120 BCE, after which both peoples saw it as a distinct religion. The temple on Gerizim is dated to the 5th century BCE; the profile keeps that in the text, outside the faith map. Another start (5th century BCE) is possible.
The article gives both a traditional account (the schism under Eli) and a scholarly one; both are reported, attributed, with no verdict.

Deportation by Assyria is 'around 720 BC' in the article's Judaism section; written as 720 BCE and attributed to the Books of Kings as read by rabbis. The article's word for the local population in that account is left out.
Priestly family: 28% in 2003 (the article gives no later figure). 'Since 1624' the oldest member is chosen High Priest.

The article gives no dates for Holon's community, no migrations, and no population figures before 2025, so the faith map has no routes and Holon's area begins in 2025 as the article's present tense. The map's Byzantine-era note and the century labels are the article's 5th-6th century revolts only.

Left out: the Hebrew, Arabic and Samaritan Hebrew name forms and the sabbath's practical details beyond the article's list; the Counting of the Omer and the Yom Teru'ah detail beyond Passover. The tenth-commandment passage is summarised, not detailed.
